extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in an introductory proofs/logic/number theory course
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and structuring elementary mathematical proofs (divisibility, congruence, absolute value, triangle inequality) and for understanding/using quantifiers and their negations. Emphasises proof techniques (direct, contrapositive, cases), modular arithmetic, and good exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrapositive in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a direct approach stalls, prove the contrapositive (e.g., to show 3 | n ⇐⇒ 3 | n^2 prove 3 ∤ n ⇒ 3 ∤ n^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try the contrapositive if assuming the forward hypothesis doesn't get you far. Example: assume 3 ∤ n, use Euclidean division to write n = 3k+1 or 3k+2 and show n^2 is not divisible by 3. Frame proofs explicitly as proving the contrapositive when using this technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases using Euclidean division (modular residues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Euclidean division to partition integers into residue classes n = 3k, 3k+1, 3k+2 (or modulo n generally) and handle each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate all possible remainders and show the claim in each case. The method simplifies many divisibility proofs; modular arithmetic can often replace tedious casework. Ensure you cover all residue classes because Euclidean division gives a unique representative for each integer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of Euclidean division as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniqueness of quotient/remainder representations allows you to rule out alternate divisibility representations (e.g., once n^2 = 3ℓ+1 you cannot also write n^2 = 3q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke Fact 3.0.3 (or the uniqueness property) to conclude that if a number has remainder r in one representation then it cannot be a multiple of the modulus. Use this to close case arguments and avoid implicit contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite divisibility statements as congruences
rubrics_metrics.description: Express divisibility using congruence notation: n ≡ 0 (mod 3) rather than '3 | n'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restating problems in congruence language often simplifies proofs and reduces casework. Example: prove n ≡ 0 (mod 3) ⇐⇒ n^2 ≡ 0 (mod 3) using properties of congruence rather than repeated Euclidean division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular arithmetic preserves arithmetic operations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a ≡ c (mod n) and b ≡ d (mod n) then a + b ≡ c + d (mod n), a − b ≡ c − d (mod n), and ab ≡ cd (mod n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the representation a = c + nk, b = d + nℓ to prove these properties. Apply them to simplify proofs (e.g., deducing n^2 residue classes from n's residue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity of congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a ≡ b (mod n) and b ≡ c (mod n) then a ≡ c (mod n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by adding the two congruence equalities (a−b = nk, b−c = nℓ) to get a−c = n(k+ℓ). Use this when chaining congruences (e.g., deducing 4 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and then substituting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use congruence to express parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parity is congruence modulo 2: a ≡ b (mod 2) iff a and b have the same parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove both implications by writing even/odd forms (2k or 2k+1). Use congruence notation to generalise parity-based arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove helpful lemmas before main theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish supporting results (lemmas) about absolute value or other basic properties before tackling the main theorem (e.g., triangle inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise proofs by deriving small lemmas (|x| ≥ 0, |x| = |−x|, −|x| ≤ x ≤ |x|, and equivalences between |x| ≤ y and −y ≤ x ≤ y) that are then reused in the main argument. This clarifies structure and reduces repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute value is a piecewise-defined function; use case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute value is defined piecewise (x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0, and sometimes presented in three cases including x=0), so proofs involving |x| typically require splitting into cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling |x| depend on the sign of x (or use symmetric three-case split x>0, x=0, x<0). The piecewise nature naturally leads to case proofs; choose the decomposition that makes the proof shortest and clearest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality proof strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y| either by direct case analysis on sign of x+y or by using prior lemmas (bounds on x and y) and adding inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two presented approaches: (1) split on whether x+y ≥ 0 or x+y < 0 and use ± representations; (2) use −|x| ≤ x ≤ |x| and −|y| ≤ y ≤ |y|, add them and apply lemma converting double inequality to absolute inequality. Choose the approach that avoids unnecessary subcases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse triangle inequality derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive bounds on |x−y| (often written as |x−y| ≥ ||x| − |y||) from the triangle inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute appropriate variables into the triangle inequality (e.g., set one variable to a and the other to b−a) and rearrange; use derived inequalities to obtain the reverse form. Show intermediate steps to avoid sign mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete examples for existential claims and counterexamples for universals
rubrics_metrics.description: To show ∃x P(x) is true, provide one explicit example; to show ∀x P(x) is false, produce a counterexample (or prove the negation ∃x ¬P(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive witness is sufficient for existence. For false universal claims, prove the negation by finding a particular value; alternatively prove the entire negation statement universally if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier punctuation and clarity of scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuate quantified statements to make the scope clear: use a comma after ∀ clauses and 'such that' (or 's.t.') after ∃ clauses; avoid embedding ∀/∃ symbols as words in running prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write ∀x ∈ A, P(x) and ∃x ∈ A s.t. P(x). Prefer the words 'for all' and 'there exists' in paragraphs to improve readability. If the domain might be ambiguous, explicitly include it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation rules for quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Negating quantifiers: ¬(∀x ∈ A, P(x)) ≡ ∃x ∈ A s.t. ¬P(x), and ¬(∃x ∈ A s.t. P(x)) ≡ ∀x ∈ A, ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disproving statements, prove the negated quantified statement. Keep the domain unchanged when negating. Use these equivalences mechanically when moving negation across quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain remains unchanged when negating quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When you negate a quantified statement the domain A stays the same; do not change to the complement domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common mistake: replacing ¬(∀x ∈ A, P(x)) with '∃x ∉ A such that P(x)'. This is incorrect. Always keep the original domain in the negated statement. Examples in text illustrate why changing domain yields false equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nested quantifiers do not commute (order matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements with nested quantifiers are not equivalent when their order is swapped: ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ≠ ∃y ∀x P(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret nested quantifiers as a two-player game (first player chooses for outer quantifier, second player responds) to test truth. Use explicit witnesses and constructions to prove or disprove statements with nested quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving statements by proving their negation
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a statement false, prove that its logical negation is true (e.g., show ∃n ¬P(n) to refute ∀n P(n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the negated quantified statement and prove it directly; this is the recommended method for demonstrating false universal claims or false existential claims (by proving the universal negation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual dropping of domains with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians often omit explicit domains when context makes them clear, but if in doubt, include domain information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reader might be unsure of the implicit domain, put in more details. The rule of thumb from the text: 'If in doubt, put in more details.' Avoid ambiguous claims by explicitly stating domains when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof style: make implicit scope explicit when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that many implications are intended universally over an (often implicit) domain; write 'for all' if the context might be unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing P(x) ⇒ Q(x), readers typically infer ∀x P(x) ⇒ Q(x) over an implied domain; but to avoid ambiguity, state the domain explicitly when necessary, especially in instructional or exam settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity/factorisation shortcuts only after justifying used facts
rubrics_metrics.description: You may shorten proofs by noting algebraic facts (e.g., n(n+1) is even), but ensure any invoked supporting results are either proved or cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example: proving n^2 + n is even by noting n(n+1) is the product of consecutive integers which includes an even factor; the text warns to prove or justify such lemmas before using them in other proofs.
